en: Thus have I heard: The Discourse to Gaṇaka Moggallāna (Majjhima Nikāya 107) Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother.
Then the brahmin Gaṇaka Moggallāna approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their courteous and amiable conversation, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the brahmin Gaṇaka Moggallāna said this to the Blessed One:
“Just as, Master Gotama, in this Palace of Migāra’s Mother, a gradual training, a gradual performance, and a gradual practice are seen— that is,
down to the lowest step of the staircase— even so, Master Gotama, among these brahmins, a gradual training, a gradual performance, and a gradual practice are seen— that is to say:”
In study as well;
for even among these archers, Master Gotama, a gradual training, a gradual performance, and a gradual practice is seen, namely, in the art of archery.
For us too, Master Gotama, among accountants who live by calculation, there is seen a gradual training, a gradual performance, and a gradual practice,
namely, in arithmetic. For when we have obtained a pupil, Master Gotama, we first teach him in this way:
“One by ones, two by twos, three by threes, four by fours, five by fives, six by sixes, seven by sevens, eight by eights, nine by nines, ten by tens”;
we could count even a hundred, Master Gotama, and more than a hundred as well.
“Is it possible, Master Gotama, to lay down such a gradual training, a gradual performance, and a gradual practice in this Dhamma and Discipline?”
“It is possible, brahmin, to prescribe a gradual training, a gradual performance, and a gradual practice in this Dhamma and Discipline.
Just as, brahmin, a skilled horse-trainer, having obtained a noble thoroughbred horse, first makes him undergo the exercise of the mouth, and afterwards makes him undergo further exercises;
even so, brahmin, when the Tathāgata obtains a person to be tamed, he first disciplines him thus:”

"Come, bhikkhu, be virtuous; dwell restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and train yourself by undertaking the rules of training.

When, brahmin, a bhikkhu is virtuous, dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, is possessed of proper conduct and resort, sees danger in even the slightest faults, and trains himself by undertaking the rules of training, then the Tathāgata disciplines him further:
"Come, bhikkhu, be one who guards the doors of the sense faculties. Upon seeing a form with the eye, do not grasp at its signs or its secondary characteristics.
Since, if one dwells with the eye faculty unguarded, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might flow in, you should practice for its restraint;
guard the eye faculty, and attain restraint over the eye faculty."
Having heard a sound with the ear …pe… having smelled an odor with the nose …pe… having tasted a flavor with the tongue …pe…
Having touched a tangible object with the body...
[and so on] ...having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, do not grasp at its signs, do not grasp at its secondary characteristics.
For if one dwells with this faculty of the mind unguarded, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might arise.

‘If, when you have gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, unwholesome states of covetousness and grief should arise in connection with mental phenomena, you should practice for their restraint; guard the mind-faculty and attain restraint over the mind-faculty.
When, brahmin, a bhikkhu is one whose sense-doors are guarded, the Tathāgata disciplines him further:
"Come, bhikkhu, be moderate in eating.
Reflecting wisely, you should take food,
neither for amusement nor for intoxication nor for the sake of physical beauty and attractiveness, but only for the maintenance and sustenance of this body."
“For the maintenance of this body, for the cessation of affliction, and for the support of the holy life—thinking:
‘Thus I shall terminate old feelings and not give rise to new feelings, and there will be for me sustenance, blamelessness, and a comfortable dwelling.
When, brahmin, a bhikkhu is moderate in eating, the Tathāgata disciplines him further:
"Come, bhikkhu, dwell devoted to wakefulness. During the day, while walking back and forth and sitting, purify your mind of obstructive states.
During the first watch of the night, while walking back and forth and sitting, purify your mind of obstructive states.
During the middle watch of the night, lie down on your right side in the lion’s posture..."
“Lay down your foot upon your foot, mindful and clearly comprehending, having directed your mind toward the perception of rising;
then, rising during the last watch of the night, purify your mind of obstructive states by means of walking and sitting.
When, brahmin, a bhikkhu is devoted to wakefulness, the Tathāgata disciplines him further:
"Come, bhikkhu, be possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension; act with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; act with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking aside;
act with clear comprehension when bending and stretching your limbs; act with clear comprehension when wearing your outer robe, bowl, and inner robe;
act with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; act with clear comprehension when defecating and urinating."
‘Whether walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, or remaining silent, he acts with clear comprehension.
When, brahmin, a bhikkhu is thus endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension, the Tathāgata further instructs him:
‘Come, bhikkhu, resort to a secluded lodging: the forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hill-cave, a charnel ground, a jungle-thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw.’”
Thus he resorts to a secluded lodging: a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw.
Having returned from his almsround after his meal, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Abandoning covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind of covetousness.
Having abandoned ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings, and purifies his mind of ill will and hatred.
Having abandoned sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, percipient of light, mindful and clearly comprehending, and purifies his mind of sloth and torpor.
Having abandoned restlessness and remorse, he dwells undisturbed, with a mind inwardly calmed, and purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse.
Having abandoned doubt, he dwells having crossed over doubt, free from uncertainty regarding wholesome states; he purifies his mind of doubt.

Having abandoned these five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—he, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and filled with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which possesses internal tranquility and singleness of mind...
With the fading away of rapture, he enters and dwells in the third jhāna...
With the abandoning of pleasure... he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.

"Brahmin, those bhikkhus who are still in training (*sekkhā*), whose minds have not yet reached their goal, and who dwell aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage— for them, I give such instruction as this.

But as for those bhikkhus who are arahants, whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained their own goal, whose fetters of existence are utterly exhausted,
and who are liberated through right gnosis— for them, these qualities [of the higher mind] are for dwelling in happiness in this very life."
“...and they lead to mindfulness and clear comprehension.
When this was said, the brahmin Gaṇaka Moggallāna said to the Blessed One:
“Now, when the Blessed Gotama’s disciples are thus exhorted and thus instructed by the Blessed Gotama, do they all attain the ultimate goal, Nibbāna, or do some not attain it?”
“Some of my disciples, brahmin, when exhorted and instructed by me in this way, attain the ultimate goal, Nibbāna; some do not attain it.

“What, Master Gotama, is the cause, what is the reason, that while Nibbāna remains, the path leading to Nibbāna remains, and Master Gotama remains as the one who encourages [others], yet some [disciples] attain it and some do not?”
"But nevertheless, some disciples of Master Gotama, being thus exhorted and thus instructed by Master Gotama, attain the ultimate goal, Nibbāna, while others do not attain it.
"In that case, brahmin, I shall question you about this very matter. Answer as you see fit.
What do you think, brahmin?"
“Are you skilled in the road leading to Rājagaha?
“Yes, sir, I am skilled in the road leading to Rājagaha.
“What do you think, brahmin?”
Suppose a man were to come here desiring to go to Rājagaha.
He would approach you and say:
"Venerable sir, I wish to go to Rājagaha."
‘Point out the way to me for that Rājagaha.
You should say to him:
‘Come, good man, this is the way that leads to Rājagaha.’”
“Go for a moment; having gone for that moment, you will see a certain village; go for a moment more; having gone for that moment, you will see a certain market town;
go for a moment more; having gone for that moment, you will see the delightful parks, the delightful groves, the delightful grounds, and the delightful lotus ponds of Rājagaha.
Being thus exhorted and instructed by you, he would take a wrong path and go westward.
Then a second man might come, desiring to go to Rājagaha.
He would approach him and say:
"Venerable sir, I wish to go to Rājagaha."
‘Point out the road to me for that Rājagaha.
You should say to him:
‘Come, good man, this is the road that leads to Rājagaha.’”
“Go for a moment; having gone for a moment, you will see a village named so-and-so.
Go for a moment; having gone for a moment, you will see a market town named so-and-so.
Go for a moment; having gone for a moment, you will see the delightful parks, the delightful groves, the delightful grounds, and the delightful lotus ponds of Rājagaha.”
"In that case, being thus exhorted and thus instructed by you, he would reach Rājagaha in safety. What, brahmin, is the cause,
what is the reason, that while Rājagaha stands, the road leading to Rājagaha stands, and you yourself stand as one who encourages,
yet when being thus exhorted and thus instructed by you, one man takes a wrong path and goes westward, while another reaches Rājagaha in safety?"
“What can I do here, Master Gotama? I am merely one who points out the path, Master Gotama.
“In the very same way, brahmin, Nibbāna stands, the path leading to Nibbāna stands, and I stand as the one who encourages others.”
"And yet, when my disciples are thus exhorted and thus instructed by me, some attain the ultimate goal, Nibbāna, while others do not.
What can I do about this, brahmin?
The Tathāgata, brahmin, is merely the proclaimer of the path."
When this was said, the brahmin Gaṇaka Moggallāna said this to the Blessed One:
"As for those persons, Master Gotama, who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of a desire for a livelihood, lacking faith— not out of faith— who are fraudulent, deceitful,
sycophantic, restless, arrogant, fickle, talkative, loose-spoken, and who do not guard the doors of their sense faculties..."
Those who are immoderate in eating, not devoted to wakefulness, indifferent to the state of a recluse, lacking intense reverence for the training,
luxurious, lax, leaders in backsliding, having abandoned the burden of seclusion, lazy, of inferior energy, muddle-minded,
lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with wandering minds, witless, and dull-witted— by them, sir, [this state] is not [attained].
Gotama dwells together with them. Furthermore,
those sons of good family who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith— being honest, free from deceit,
not guileful, not arrogant, not haughty, not fickle, not boisterous, not loose-tongued, guarding the doors of their sense faculties, and moderate in eating— [dwell together with him].
Devoted to wakefulness, looking toward the state of a recluse, possessing intense reverence for the training, not given to abundance, not given to indolence,
having laid aside the burden of worldly decline, taking the lead in solitude, with energy aroused, resolute, established in mindfulness,
clearly comprehending, concentrated, one-pointed in mind, wise, and not dull-witted— Master Gotama dwells together with such as these.
"Just as, Master Gotama, of all root-fragrances, black aloe is declared the foremost;
of all heartwood-fragrances, red sandalwood is declared the foremost;
of all flower-fragrances, jasmine is declared the foremost."
In this very way, the instruction of Master Gotama regarding the supreme Dhamma is excellent.
Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!
Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost...
Or one who might show the way, or one who might hold up an oil lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
just so has the Dhamma been made clear by Master Gotama in many ways.
Therefore, I go for refuge to Master Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
The Gaṇakamoggallāna Sutta is finished; it is the seventh.
